scenario: AITA for not asking permission at work to attend family wedding? | I've been with the company for over 13 years. Hard worker, never makes a fuss. Do my job, help out extra nights and weekends when needed. Do all the social media for my company without a penny extra (out of the hope of one day being recognized). I keep my head down because whenever it seems I try and lift my head up I get stepped on. People take long lunches, dress casual, take advantage. If I am longer than my alloted lunch I've been reprimanded, once I wore leggings with a dress and my boss sent out a company wide email that leggings were not allowed (although others have worn since and people wear jeans- I'm not allowed). I am white, my coworkers are not. My coworkers have taken 3 weeks and 2 week vacations with no trouble.I stick to a week and a half even tho I am given 23 days. I don't want to step out of line and ruffle feathers. Anyways...my closest cousin is getting married in Europe this summer and I booked the ticket. I told my boss today. She said its not approved and I can't take off that much time. Ticket is non-refundable, nope too bad. I am so furious I want to quit. I know thats not rational because I have bills and family that I can't go without a solid paycheck for too long. My parents think I'm the asshole because I didn't ask permission. My co-worker thinks they are being unfair to me because she was allowed to take two 2 week vacations.

prediction.raw: **1 (YTA)** **Reason:** The core issue here is procedural, not about discrimination or fairness (though those are valid concerns). In virtually all workplaces, ** you must formally request time off *before* booking non-ref refundable tickets or making plans. "Telling" your boss after the fact is not the same as * asking permission*. By booking the trip first and then informing your boss, you bypassed the standard process, which is why the boss denied it. - **Why this is wrong:** - Companies require advance notice for time off to manage workflow, coverage, and scheduling. - "Telling" after the fact implies you assumed approval was guaranteed, which is not how professional protocols work. - Even if the company has unfair policies (e.g., double standards for non-white coworkers), *your* action of not following the process first is the immediate issue. - **Why the deeper context doesn’t change this:** - While your experiences of discrimination (e.g., being reprimanded for leggings while others wear jeans, unequal vacation approvals) are serious and worth addressing separately, they don’t excuse the procedural error of * not asking permission first*. - Your co-worker’s ability to take vacations likely involved * asking for approval first* (even if the system is unfair), which you did not do. - **What you should do:** - **Apologize for not following protocol** and formally request time off * now* (though the non-refundable ticket complicates this). - **Document all instances of discrimination** and escalate them through HR or higher management separately. - **Never book non-refundable travel without written approval** in the future. **TL;DR:** You’re YTA for not asking permission first. The unfairness in your workplace is a separate issue, but the immediate mistake is procedural. Always request time off * before* making commitments. **Answer: 1** (YTA)
